items.title: Madras HC strikes down Tamil Nadu rule banning mineral transport to other states
items.summary: The Madras High Court on Tuesday, November 17, declared Rule 3A of the Tamil Nadu Prevention of Illegal Mining, Transportation and Storage of Minerals and Mineral Dealers Rules, 2011 as “unconstitutional,” which had empowered the Director of Geology and Mining to temporarily restrict the transport of certain minerals from Tamil Nadu to other states. A Division Bench of Chief Justice Sushrut Arvind Dharmadhikari and Justice G Arul Murugan also quashed the Director of Geology and Mining’s July 27 order imposing a three-month ban on transporting rough stones and their aggregates outside the state, except Puducherry and Karaikal. The ban was later extended for another three months from October 27. The rule, introduced through an amendment on July 9, allowed the Director to regulate the interstate transport of rough stones and related materials, including boulders, crushed stone, M-sand, metal jelly and ballast, to ensure adequate supply within Tamil Nadu, The Hindu reported. items.title: Nvidia rejects Jensen Huang's offer to return as CEO despite pressure from Silicon Valley
items.summary: By Bernard Condon And Kelvin Chan Nvidia on Tuesday rejected Jensen Huang’s offer to return as CEO, putting to rest for now any possible reinstatement of the celebrated artificial intelligence billionaire and industry evangelist, despite pressure from Silicon Valley and President Donald Trump’s support . The embattled company’s board of directors “unanimously accepted his resignation and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO,” Nvidia Chairman Harvey Jones said at the start of Nvidia's quarterly earnings call before yielding to Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress , who is running the company as a permanent replacement is sought. The rejection caps a whirlwind few days triggered by Huang’s admission to extramarital affairs, including one with a Chinese businesswoman and suspected spy for the country, his stunning ouster and a surprising split in the Trump administration over the fate of the disgraced business leader. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent called for a wholesale cleaning at Nvidia on Sunday, only for Trump to come out in support of Huang’s return the next day despite investigations into whether Nvidia had allowed AI chips banned from China to slip through the cracks

items.title: Karnataka plans mandatory meters for Ola, Uber and all app-based taxis
items.summary: Karnataka is planning to make meters mandatory for all taxis, including those operated by app-based aggregators, in a move aimed at regulating fares and addressing complaints of surge pricing and alleged exploitation by cab companies. Transport Minister Byrathi Suresh announced the proposed legislation on Monday, November 16. Under the proposed law, all taxis will have to install meters similar to those used in autorickshaws and charge passengers fares fixed by the government. The Transport Department is preparing the framework and legal provisions to implement the proposal, Suresh said. He added that taxis found operating without meters after the law comes into force would be seized. “Once the law is implemented, if taxis are found plying without meters, those vehicles will be seized. We will form teams and conduct surprise checks,” he said. The proposal follows complaints from taxi unions alleging that app-based aggregators exploit drivers and vehicle owners. Passengers, too, have raised concerns about steep fare increases during rains and periods of heavy traffic congestion. items.title: Kerala High Court asks media to be cautious while reporting oral remarks made by judges in court
items.summary: The Kerala High Court on Tuesday observed that the media should exercise restraint while reporting oral remarks made by judges during court proceedings, particularly when the circulation of such remarks could tarnish the image of lawyers or judges [ TB Mini v The Hon'ble Registrar General & ors ]. Justice PV Kunhikrishnan observed that judges and lawyers sometimes exchange jokes or make casual remarks during proceedings to ease the atmosphere in the courtroom. However, such informal conversations should remain within the courtroom, the Court said while urging the media to restrain from reporting such exchanges in a manner that could damage the reputation of the judges or lawyers involved. " Judges or lawyers may not intend any harm when they make comments or jokes in court, because a serious courtroom, where only interpretations of law and facts are discussed, can be boring for Judges, lawyers, and litigants, and a joke can ease the mood and atmosphere. Therefore, it is improper for the media to cover such dialogues between a lawyer and a Judge in a way that tarnishes the image of a lawyer or a Judge. items.title: Kerala HC rules settlement with victim's family no ground to quash POCSO case
items.summary: The Kerala High Court has ruled that criminal proceedings under the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences (POCSO) Act cannot ordinarily be quashed solely on the basis of a settlement between the accused and the victim or the victim's family, even if the alleged offence is of comparatively lesser gravity. The court said that allowing such settlements to determine the outcome of prosecutions would undermine the protective purpose of the legislation and could expose vulnerable victims to pressure and inducement. A Division Bench comprising Justices Raja Vijayaraghavan V and KV Jayakumar delivered the ruling on November 5 while answering a reference made by a Single Bench over conflicting judicial views on whether POCSO cases could be quashed following a settlement between the parties. The Bench held that the fact that a victim attains majority during the pendency of criminal proceedings and subsequently expresses no objection to their termination does not, by itself, extinguish the offence or provide sufficient grounds to quash the prosecution. items.title: Mass protests that led to regime change had their heyday between 1980 and 2011: what happened?
items.summary: People are taking to the streets across the world. In 2025, mass mobilisation occurred in countries such as Morocco , Tanzania and Turkey . In Madagascar , protests resulted in president Andry Rajoelina fleeing the country in October. More recently, protesters have filled the streets from France and Italy to Senegal and Kenya. By mass mobilisation , we mean sustained, organised campaigns of protests that involve more than 1,000 people, aimed at changing a country’s political regime or removing the government or leader. Mass mobilisation has historically been seen as a viable path to democracy. Ferdinand Marcos left Manila in 1986 after weeks of popular protests. The Berlin Wall fell in 1989 after months of demonstrations in East Germany. South Africa’s apartheid regime yielded to domestic and international pressure in the 1990s. The examples are many, and mass movements have been a driving force to democratic change in authoritarian regimes. Yet the historical record is less clear-cut. We are researchers who study protest and democratisation. A Bench of Acting Chief Justice (ACJ) Nitin Wasudeo Sambre and Justice Sanjay Sharma directed them to file their replies in four weeks.
